prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency.

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part B048 configuration with Katori and Ye, and the first-round exchange has strengthened rather than weakened it. The physical core is not disputed by anyone: the magic-wavelength condition cancels the lattice light shift while many atoms sit in the Lamb-Dicke regime, giving Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation with a large signal-to-noise advantage. What makes it a physics result and not only an instrument is what followed: clocks near 1e-18 reproduced in several laboratories and species, millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on drifting constants and ultralight dark matter, and the discovery that spin-exchange and many-body interactions between the atoms matter at this precision and can be controlled. On the chair's chronology question, my recollection, which I flag as memory and not a check of primary papers, is that Katori and collaborators proposed the magic-wavelength lattice trapping scheme in 2003, that the first strontium lattice clock operation came from Katori's group around 2003 to 2005, and that Ye's group (with Boyd, Ludlow and others) delivered the systematic accuracy record and the many-body understanding in the following years. That ordering supports the split of concept and first realisation on one side and accuracy and many-body physics on the other, and I would not change the two-name credit. The citation should name only the lattice clock, so that it stays visibly distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
statement.case_against: The central objection survives my reflection: a sceptical member can call the lattice clock the next step of a lineage the Academy has honoured twice, and can say it is metrology rather than a new phenomenon. My answer is a mechanism argument (many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, a different route from single-ion control or from the comb as a frequency ruler) and the many-body results, but it remains a judgement, not a fact. Credit is also simplified by two names: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Boyd, Hollberg and the Yb, Hg and ion-clock groups made real contributions, and I cannot adjudicate their priority from memory. Finally, the redefinition of the second is pending, so the full practical consequence is still ahead.

responses.point: The lattice clock is a fundamental result and not merely technological, in the way high-harmonic generation was a clean idea in atomic structure that became a new way to see nature.
responses.response: I agree with the analogy and with the claim that the physics is in the use, not the device. Where I would sharpen it is the distinction from 2005 and 2012. The comb gave a ruler for optical frequencies and ion control gave single quantum systems with very small shifts. The lattice clock is a different mechanism: interrogating thousands of neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, which brings statistical power and, as a consequence, many-body effects that single-ion clocks do not have. I would therefore keep the citation narrow around the lattice clock and not cite 'time and frequency at the 10^-18 level' alone, since that wording could read as a continuation of earlier prizes. I take the 10^-18 figure as supporting evidence, not as the achievement.

responses.point: The EHT (B052) has the greatest existential reach on the list, but the clock is the more defensible prize, and the redefinition of the second leaves timing open.
responses.response: I respect the choice to trade excitement for defensibility, and I would not call it a loss of scientific nerve. I defer to you on the astrophysics, but from where I sit the shadow-size test of gravity looks model dependent, and the imaging credit leaves out the algorithm and station leaders you mention. On timing, I hold that the redefinition of the second should be neither a reason to wait nor a reason to act. The lattice clocks have been reproduced at 1e-18 across laboratories already, so the science does not depend on the SI decision. If you hold timing as open, I would ask what additional evidence you would need that is not already in the clock comparisons.

responses.point: Mehlig would be more concerned if either Katori or Ye were dropped than about the split between them, and now judges KPZ (B011) unlikely this year.
responses.response: I agree that dropping either name would be the larger error, and I do not see a case for a third name. Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow are important, but nothing I recall gives any of them a claim that outweighs Katori's concept and first realisation or Ye's accuracy and many-body work, and a third name would need a documented ground, not a general sense of fairness. I also take your point that B011 has a credit problem with Parisi and the exact solutions. For the record, I have moved my alternatives accordingly and no longer list circuit QED among them, for the conflict reason in my note.

responses.point: Waiting for the redefinition of the second risks a missed or contested attribution as the field grows, and a second prize part is not useful because B025 has a contested credit.
responses.response: I agree on both. A larger lattice-clock community makes the credit harder to hold at two names, so the cleanest moment is when the founders are identifiable. On a second part, I do not see a candidate that fits within three people in total, as Lindroth observed, since B048 already takes two names and B025 would take three more. I would only support a second part if a candidate had a single exact name or two, and none of the shortlist does. Since you and Lindroth are closest to the primary clock papers, I would welcome a check of the 2003 to 2005 chronology from you before the vote.

uncertainties: Whether the full committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; this is a judgement and I cannot settle it as a fact.
Exact priority chronology between Katori's 2003 to 2005 work and the Ye group's later accuracy milestones; I am recalling from memory and have not checked primary papers.
Whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Boyd or others have a claim strong enough to join the two names; I think not, but I cannot prove it.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should affect timing; I hold it should not.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: circuit QED (B001) is the architecture of my own research and of the WACQT programme I direct, and its credited names are close colleagues. I would recuse myself from discussion and ballot on B001 or any configuration containing it, and I have therefore dropped it from my alternatives. This does not touch the B048-only configuration. I know of no tie to Katori or Ye beyond belonging to the same broad community of quantum-technology researchers.
